concepts.name: Natural Carbon Cycle: Reservoirs and Fluxes
key_dimensions: Four major carbon reservoirs: atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere — sizes and residence times
Key fluxes: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, ocean-atmosphere exchange — natural balance vs. current imbalance
Distinction between fast carbon cycle (biological) and slow carbon cycle (geological) — timescales and disruption points
UPSC trap: Ocean is the largest active carbon sink, but lithosphere holds the largest total carbon stock — common confusion

concepts.name: Anthropogenic Carbon Emissions: Sources and Relative Contributions
key_dimensions: Sectoral breakdown: energy (largest), agriculture, industry, transport, land-use change — IPCC data points
Distinction between CO2 and non-CO2 GHGs (CH4, N2O) in carbon cycle disruption context
Cumulative vs. annual emissions: relevance to historical responsibility and climate negotiations (CBDR principle)
UPSC trap: Deforestation is both a carbon source AND reduces future sink capacity — dual disruption mechanism

concepts.name: Terrestrial Carbon Sinks: Forests, Soils, and Wetlands
key_dimensions: Tropical vs. temperate vs. boreal forests — carbon density differences and vulnerability profiles
Soil organic carbon (SOC): largest terrestrial carbon pool, role of permafrost, threat from warming and tilling
Wetlands and peatlands: disproportionate carbon storage relative to area; drainage converts them from sink to source
UPSC trap: Wetlands store carbon as peat but also emit CH4 — net GHG effect depends on context (temperature, water level)

concepts.name: Ocean Carbon Sink: Mechanisms and Saturation Risk
key_dimensions: Two pumps: solubility pump (CO2 dissolves in cold water) and biological pump (phytoplankton photosynthesis → sinking organic matter)
Ocean acidification as a co-consequence of carbon absorption — impact on calcifying organisms and biological pump efficiency
Sink saturation: warming reduces CO2 solubility; evidence that Southern Ocean and North Atlantic sinks are weakening
UPSC trap: Oceans absorb ~25–30% of anthropogenic CO2 annually but this absorption is declining proportionally — sink-to-source transition risk

concepts.name: Ocean Acidification: Chemistry, Impacts, and Policy Linkages
key_dimensions: Chemical mechanism: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H⁺ + HCO3⁻ — pH has dropped from 8.2 to ~8.1 (30% more acidic in H⁺ terms)
Biological impacts: coral bleaching vs. dissolution, pteropods, oysters — distinction between bleaching (temperature) and dissolution (pH)
Feedback loop: degraded coral reefs → reduced biological pump → less carbon sequestration
UPSC trap: Ocean acidification is NOT caused by temperature rise — it is a direct chemical effect of CO2 absorption, independent of warming per se

concepts.name: Permafrost Carbon Feedback: A Climate Tipping Point
key_dimensions: Permafrost stores ~1,500 Gt of organic carbon — nearly double current atmospheric CO2 stock
Thawing releases both CO2 (aerobic decomposition) and CH4 (anaerobic in waterlogged areas) — CH4 is 80× more potent over 20 years
Self-reinforcing feedback: warming → thaw → emissions → more warming — classic positive feedback loop
UPSC trap: Permafrost carbon release is NOT included in most IPCC baseline scenarios — actual warming may exceed projections (missing feedback)

concepts.name: Deforestation and Land-Use Change: Carbon Flux Implications
key_dimensions: Deforestation contributes ~10–15% of global GHG emissions (IPCC AR6) — third largest source after energy and agriculture
Carbon debt concept: when forests are cleared and burned, stored carbon is instantly released; regrowth takes decades to recapture
REDD+ mechanism: Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation — additionality, permanence, leakage as key challenges
UPSC trap: Afforestation ≠ Reforestation ≠ Forest restoration — UPSC frequently tests definitional distinctions and their carbon implications

concepts.name: Carbon Feedback Loops: Positive vs. Negative Feedbacks
key_dimensions: Positive feedbacks amplifying warming: ice-albedo feedback, water vapor feedback, permafrost methane, forest dieback
Negative feedbacks dampening warming: increased plant growth with CO2 fertilization (CO2 fertilization effect), increased cloud cover (uncertain)
Tipping points vs. gradual feedbacks — irreversibility threshold and policy urgency
UPSC trap: CO2 fertilization effect (plants grow faster with more CO2) is a negative feedback but is OFFSET by warming, drought, and nutrient limitations — not a reliable long-term sink

concepts.name: Methane (CH4) in the Carbon Cycle: Sources, Sinks, and Policy Gaps
key_dimensions: Sources: wetlands (natural), livestock enteric fermentation, rice paddies, fossil fuel extraction, landfills — natural vs. anthropogenic split
GWP (Global Warming Potential): CH4 = 84× CO2 over 20 years, 28× over 100 years — policy implications of time horizon choice
Global Methane Pledge (COP26): 30% reduction by 2030 from 2020 levels — who signed, who didn't (China and India notably absent initially)
UPSC trap: CH4 has a shorter atmospheric lifetime (~12 years vs. CO2's centuries) — cutting CH4 gives faster near-term climate benefit; relevant for 1.5°C target

concepts.name: Blue Carbon Ecosystems: Mangroves, Seagrasses, and Salt Marshes
key_dimensions: Carbon sequestration rates: mangroves sequester carbon 3–5× faster per unit area than tropical forests — stored in biomass AND sediment
Distinction: Blue carbon stored in sediments is millennia-old and relatively stable; destruction releases this legacy carbon rapidly
India-specific: Sundarbans, Andaman mangroves — India's NDC and blue carbon potential
UPSC trap: Blue carbon ecosystems are NOT yet formally included in UNFCCC national accounting frameworks for most countries — a current policy gap

concepts.name: Carbon Budget: Concept, Remaining Budget, and 1.5°C Implications
key_dimensions: Definition: total CO2 that can be emitted while limiting warming to 1.5°C or 2°C — IPCC AR6 estimates ~400–500 Gt CO2 remaining for 1.5°C (as of 2023)
Carbon budget fairness: per-capita vs. historical emissions basis — developed vs. developing country perspectives
Budget overshoot and negative emissions: if budget is exceeded, CDR (Carbon Dioxide Removal) becomes mandatory — moral hazard risk
UPSC trap: Carbon budget is probabilistic (67% chance of staying below 1.5°C), not a guaranteed threshold — UPSC may test the probabilistic nature

concepts.name: Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) Technologies: Natural vs. Technological
key_dimensions: Nature-based CDR: afforestation, soil carbon sequestration, biochar, blue carbon — co-benefits and limitations (land use, permanence)
Technological CDR: DACCS (Direct Air Carbon Capture and Storage), BECCS (Bioenergy with CCS) — energy intensive, costly, unproven at scale
BECCS paradox: requires vast land for bioenergy crops, competing with food production and biodiversity — sustainability trade-off
UPSC trap: CDR is different from Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) at emission point — CCS prevents new emissions; CDR removes existing CO2 from atmosphere

concepts.name: Carbon Sinks to Sources: Forest Dieback and Amazon Tipping Point
key_dimensions: Amazon dieback hypothesis: ~20–25% deforestation could trigger savannization — regional rainfall disruption via 'flying rivers'
Current status: Parts of eastern Amazon are already net carbon sources (2021 Science study) — policy urgency
Interaction of deforestation + climate warming + fire frequency — compound stress exceeding ecosystem resilience
UPSC trap: Amazon acting as a carbon source does NOT mean all forests are — distinguishing regional specificity from global generalization

concepts.name: Carbon Cycle and Agriculture: Emissions and Sequestration Potential
key_dimensions: Agriculture contributes ~18–23% of GHGs: CH4 from livestock and rice, N2O from fertilizers, CO2 from land use change
Soil carbon sequestration potential: conservation tillage, cover crops, agroforestry — '4 per 1000' initiative (France, COP21)
Trade-off: intensification reduces land pressure (sparing) vs. organic farming sequesters more carbon but needs more land (sharing) — unresolved debate
UPSC trap: N2O (from fertilizers) has GWP of 265× CO2 over 100 years and is NOT the same as NOx — a common confusion in prelims

concepts.name: Carbon Pricing Mechanisms: Carbon Tax vs. Cap-and-Trade
key_dimensions: Carbon tax: price certainty but quantity uncertainty; cap-and-trade: quantity certainty but price uncertainty — fundamental trade-off
EU Emissions Trading System (ETS): world's largest carbon market, carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) — implications for India's exports
Article 6 of Paris Agreement: international carbon markets — Article 6.2 (bilateral) vs. 6.4 (multilateral UNFCCC mechanism) — Glasgow/Dubai negotiations
UPSC trap: India's Perform Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme is an energy efficiency market, NOT a carbon market per se — frequently confused

concepts.name: Net Zero vs. Carbon Neutrality vs. Climate Neutrality: Definitional Distinctions
key_dimensions: Net zero CO2: emissions balanced by CDR for CO2 only; carbon neutrality: includes offsets (may not require actual reductions); climate neutrality: all GHGs balanced
India's NDC and Net Zero 2070 target — what it covers, what it excludes, comparison with China (2060) and developed nations (2050)
Corporate net zero claims vs. Paris-aligned net zero — greenwashing risk and lack of standardized verification
UPSC trap: Net zero ≠ zero emissions — residual emissions are permitted if balanced by equivalent removals; and carbon offsets can mask continued emissions

concepts.name: Albedo, Black Carbon, and Short-Lived Climate Pollutants (SLCPs)
key_dimensions: Black carbon (soot): absorbs solar radiation, deposits on ice reducing albedo — warming effect despite short atmospheric lifetime (~weeks)
Sources of black carbon: diesel vehicles, biomass burning, brick kilns — disproportionate impact in Himalayas and Arctic
SLCPs include: black carbon, CH4, tropospheric ozone, HFCs — Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) as governance mechanism

UPSC trap: Black carbon is not a GHG in the traditional sense (it doesn't trap longwave radiation) but contributes to warming through direct absorption and albedo reduction — mechanism distinction matters

concepts.name: Carbon Sequestration in India: Policies, Targets, and Challenges
key_dimensions: India's NDC target: create additional carbon sink of 2.5–3 billion tonnes CO2 equivalent through forest and tree cover by 2030
Green India Mission under NAPCC: 5 million hectares of forest restoration — funding gap and implementation challenges
Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act (CAMPA): funds from diversion of forest land — quality of compensatory plantations vs. natural forests

UPSC trap: India's carbon sink target is stated in CO2 equivalent absorbed, not in area terms — monoculture plantations count toward area but have far lower carbon and biodiversity value than natural forests

concepts.name: IPCC Carbon Cycle Findings: AR6 Key Conclusions and Policy Linkages
key_dimensions: AR6 WG1 finding: land and ocean sinks have absorbed ~56% of anthropogenic emissions but their efficiency is declining
1.5°C vs. 2°C carbon cycle differences: at 2°C, risk of carbon cycle feedbacks causing further 0.1–0.3°C additional warming
Carbon cycle in 'overshoot' scenarios: temporary exceedance of 1.5°C requires large-scale CDR to return — feasibility and justice concerns

UPSC trap: IPCC does not make policy recommendations — it assesses science. Policy decisions rest with UNFCCC/governments. This distinction between scientific assessment and policy prescription is a recurring UPSC angle
